settings.title: Settings
help.panel.title: Panel
help.panel.body:
A left click on the tray icon opens the panel: tunnels on the left, the PCs behind each tunnel on the right, PCs without a tunnel last. The marker next to a name shows the state: green working, yellow in progress (blinking), blue off, grey outline unknown, red the last action failed.

A left click on a tunnel or PC opens its actions, a right click its details. Sleep and shut down run only after a confirming second click. The screen of the tray icon shows the PCs as a whole, the corner square the tunnels; its tooltip says how many tunnels are up and how many PCs are online.
help.wake.title: Waking
help.wake.body:
"Wake" on a PC behind a tunnel first brings the tunnel up and then sends the wake request. There are three ways: a relay host in the PC's network over SSH (RouterOS, etherwake or wakeonlan), a magic packet from this computer to any address, or a command of your own. A PC counts as on when all of its readiness ports answer.

The program never drops a tunnel by itself, only the tunnel button does, so an RDP session or a copy it does not know about is never cut.
help.power.title: Sleep and shut down
help.power.body: Sleep and shut down are available while the PC is online. Over SSH the program sends a fixed command to the PC: on Linux sudo systemctl suspend -i or sudo systemctl poweroff, on Windows SetSuspendState or shutdown /s. The wizard shows the commands to run once on the PC (the key and the sudo rule). Commands of your own are possible too.
help.settings.title: Settings
help.settings.body: Everything is stored in config.toml next to the program (or in the file given with --config). The settings window and the wizard change only the values that changed, so comments and the order of lines stay. The file can be edited by hand as well; settings saved in the window apply at once. HomeLink.exe --check-config checks the file and lists every problem.
help.ssh.title: SSH and keys
help.ssh.body:
Relay hosts and PCs are reached with the system OpenSSH client and a key only, never a password. On Windows 10 LTSC the OpenSSH client may be missing: Settings > Apps > Optional features > OpenSSH Client.

"Create key" in the wizard makes a key in the keys folder next to the settings. A host key is added to known_hosts only after you compared the fingerprint and pressed "Trust"; the program never replaces a changed host key.
help.rdp.title: Remote Desktop
help.rdp.body: The RDP button opens mstsc with the file rdp\<PC id>.rdp, which is made on first use and never rewritten (so it can be signed). The password is typed in the Remote Desktop window: HomeLink never sees or stores it.
help.files.title: Program files
help.files.body: Next to config.toml are: the log homelink.log (up to 1 MB, two older copies), the lock file homelink.lock (stops a second copy), the keys folder with SSH keys and the rdp folder with Remote Desktop files. The program runs with administrator rights because the WireGuard tunnel service needs them.
help.privacy.title: Privacy
help.privacy.body: HomeLink stores no passwords, sends no telemetry and checks for no updates. It connects only to the hosts in its settings: it checks ports, reads the tunnel's handshake (or pings its probe host), sends magic packets, connects over SSH and runs the commands you gave.

wizard.ssh.already_known: known_hosts already has an entry for {host}. HomeLink never replaces an entry. If the device was reinstalled and you are sure, remove the old entry with: ssh-keygen -R {host}
wizard.ssh.host_key_changed: The host key of {host} differs from the one stored in known_hosts. The device may have been reinstalled, or something else is answering in its place. HomeLink never replaces a key by itself.

wizard.rdp.note: HomeLink never handles the Remote Desktop password. Type it in the Remote Desktop window; Windows can remember it there.
wizard.wake.relay: Through a relay host over SSH (a router or an always-on device in the PC's network)
wizard.relay.setup.routeros: Run these commands on the router. They create a group that can only log in over SSH and run /tool wol, and a user in it that can log in only from this computer's address, with a random password that nobody knows (RouterOS requires one; with the default password-authentication=yes-if-no-key a user with a key cannot log in with a password anyway), add the public key and enable the user. Replace anything in <angle brackets>. Checked on RouterOS 7.24.
wizard.relay.setup.etherwake: Run these commands on the relay host as root; the user must already exist. They install etherwake and add the public key to the user's authorized_keys. On OpenWrt use opkg install etherwake instead. If sudo is on, the last two lines let that user run this one program with sudo without a password. Replace anything in <angle brackets>.
wizard.relay.setup.wakeonlan: Run these commands on the relay host as root; the user must already exist. They install wakeonlan and add the public key to the user's authorized_keys. If sudo is on, the last two lines let that user run this one program with sudo without a password. Replace anything in <angle brackets>.
wizard.pc.setup.linux: Run these commands on the PC as root; the user must already exist. They add the public key to the user's authorized_keys and let that user run exactly the two commands HomeLink sends (systemctl poweroff and systemctl suspend -i) with sudo without a password. Replace anything in <angle brackets>.
wizard.pc.setup.windows: Run these commands on the PC in PowerShell as administrator. They install and start the OpenSSH server and add the public key for administrators; the user must be an administrator of the PC, because shutting it down over SSH needs that right. Not yet verified on every Windows version: check the result with the check on the last step.
wizard.hint.sudo: Turn it on when the SSH user is not root and the tool needs root. HomeLink runs `sudo -n`, which never asks for a password, so sudo must be allowed without one.
wizard.magic.routed_help: To wake a PC in a routed network or another VLAN, use the PC's own IP address as the destination and add a static ARP entry for it (with its MAC address) on the router closest to the PC. A subnet broadcast address works only if that router forwards directed broadcasts.
wizard.test.note: The PC can be saved even if a check fails.
wizard.hint.windows_sleep: On Windows, sleep hibernates the PC when hibernation is enabled.
